name: Central Air Conditioner
blurb: Central AC is usually the single largest electricity user in homes that have it, with compressors drawing 2–5 kW while running. In hot climates it can account for well over half of a summer bill, which makes runtime — not the unit itself — the thing to manage.
tips: Each degree you raise the thermostat trims cooling costs by roughly 2–3%.
Replace filters and hose off the outdoor coil each season — restricted airflow directly raises wattage.
Ceiling fans let most people stay comfortable ~3°F warmer, and cost pennies a day by comparison.

name: Window Air Conditioner
blurb: Window units draw 500–1,500 watts depending on size, and cooling a single occupied room this way is far cheaper than running central air for the whole house. Efficiency varies widely — a modern inverter unit can halve the cost of a decade-old one.
tips: Buy the right size: an oversized unit short-cycles, dehumidifies poorly, and wastes energy.
Seal the gaps around the mounting panels — leaks pull in hot outdoor air continuously.
Use 'eco' or 'auto' mode so the compressor cycles off at temperature instead of running flat out.

name: Portable Air Conditioner
blurb: Portable ACs are the least efficient common cooling option — single-hose designs pull conditioned air out of the room, so more of every kilowatt-hour is wasted compared with a window unit of the same rating. Expect meaningfully higher costs for the same cooling.

name: Ductless Mini-Split
blurb: Inverter-driven mini-splits are the efficiency benchmark for room cooling, sipping a few hundred watts once a room reaches temperature instead of cycling a big compressor. They typically cool the same space for one-third to one-half the cost of window or portable units.

name: Ceiling Fan
blurb: A ceiling fan uses about as much power as a bright light bulb — roughly 1–2% of what central AC draws. Fans cool people, not rooms, so the savings come from raising the AC setpoint a few degrees, then switching the fan off when you leave.

name: Box Fan
blurb: A 20-inch box fan on high draws well under 100 watts, making it one of the cheapest cooling tools available. Running one all night long costs a few cents in most states — a rounding error next to any air conditioner.

name: Tower Fan
blurb: Tower fans trade a little airflow efficiency for quiet and footprint, drawing 40–100 watts. Like all fans, they're dramatically cheaper than refrigerated cooling — the cost decision is really about which fan you'll actually leave on.

name: Whole-House Fan
blurb: A whole-house fan flushes hot indoor air out through the attic on cool evenings, drawing a few hundred watts instead of a few thousand. In dry climates with cool nights it can replace hours of AC runtime a day.

name: Attic Fan
blurb: Powered attic ventilators draw 200–500 watts to lower attic temperatures. Their net savings are debated — in leaky homes they can pull conditioned air upward — so seal the attic floor before counting on them to cut cooling bills.

name: Evaporative (Swamp) Cooler
blurb: In dry climates, evaporative coolers deliver whole-room cooling for fan-level wattage — typically 100–800 watts, a quarter or less of comparable AC. The tradeoff is water use and poor performance anywhere humid.

name: Dehumidifier
blurb: A dehumidifier is a small heat pump that often runs 10+ hours a day in damp basements, quietly becoming one of the house's bigger consumers. Newer Energy Star units with humidistats cost roughly 30% less to run than older always-on models.
tips: Set the humidistat to 50% rather than 'continuous' — every extra point of dryness costs real kWh.
Empty or gravity-drain the tank so the unit never idles full while the compressor cycles.
Seal basement leaks and downspouts first; drier inflow means fewer runtime hours.

name: Humidifier
blurb: Cool-mist and ultrasonic humidifiers draw modest power — often 20–50 watts — but warm-mist models that boil water can reach 300 watts. Model choice, not runtime, is the main cost lever here.
